title: Probability, impact, proximity, velocity and exposure
blurb: Define probability, impact, proximity, velocity and exposure, and use them to decide which risks matter most.
question: A risk could strike in month 9, and if it does, it would hit the budget within hours. Which measure describes 'month 9', and which describes 'within hours'?

teach.body: Formally: risk probability is the estimated chance that a risk will occur; risk impact is the estimated effect on objectives should it occur. Probability is often estimated from the probability or frequency of occurrence. Impact is expressed in the same units as the objective it affects, such as days or pounds. In plain English: how likely is it, and how much would it hurt (or help)?

teach.caption: The scales themselves are defined in the risk management approach, so everyone rates risks the same way.

teach.h: Proximity and velocity: two kinds of time
teach.body: Risk proximity is how near in time a risk might occur: next week, or in stage 4? Risk velocity, new in PRINCE2 7, is how quickly the risk would have an impact on objectives should it occur: does the damage arrive in hours or build over months? A far-off risk can still have high velocity, and a near risk can creep in slowly.

teach.h: Exposure: how much is at risk
teach.body: Risk exposure is the degree to which a particular objective is 'at risk'. It is a neutral concept, because exposure can be positive (opportunities) or negative (threats). Looking across all risks gives the combined (aggregated) risk exposure, which is compared with risk tolerance and the business's risk appetite, and checked against the business case.

teach.caption: A common way to compare risks is expected value: probability multiplied by impact. Opportunities count too.
The combined picture is assessed against tolerance; a forecast breach would be escalated.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a hospital pharmacy system
teach.body: At Fenmoor Health Trust, project manager Grace Okafor is assessing a threat that the new dispensing software may fail regulatory sign-off. Probability: medium. Impact: three months' delay and £60k. Proximity: stage 3, about five months away. Velocity: high, because a failed sign-off would stop go-live instantly. Grace notes that although the risk is not close, its velocity means a contingent plan must be ready before stage 3 starts.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Proximity is WHEN a risk might occur; velocity is HOW QUICKLY it would affect objectives once it occurs. (2) Exposure is neutral: it can be positive or negative. (3) Impact is measured in the units of the objective affected (days, pounds), not just 'high' or 'low' for its own sake.

items: Probability: estimated chance of occurring (probability or frequency).
Impact: estimated effect on objectives, in the objective's units.
Proximity: how near in time the risk might occur.
Velocity (new): how quickly it would affect objectives once it occurs.
Exposure: degree to which an objective is at risk; neutral; aggregated exposure is compared with tolerance.

summary: You can now define probability, impact, proximity, velocity and exposure, and use them to rank risks. You can also tell proximity (when) from velocity (how fast) and explain how aggregated exposure is compared with risk tolerance.

options: How quickly a risk would affect objectives
How closely the risk owner monitors it
How likely it is that a risk will occur
How near in time a risk might occur
A.why: Risk proximity is how near in time a risk might occur (manual 9.2).

whyNot.1: Monitoring is part of implementing responses, not a measure of the risk.

options: How quickly a risk would affect objectives if it occurs
How many risks are added to the register each stage
How fast a planned risk response can be put into action
How often a risk has occurred on earlier projects
A.why: Velocity, new in PRINCE2 7, is how quickly a risk would have an impact on objectives should it occur.

whyNot.1: The rate of new risks is not a defined measure of a single risk.
whyNot.2: Velocity is about the risk's impact, not the response.
whyNot.3: Frequency of past occurrence helps estimate probability, not velocity.

A.q: In which units should risk impact be expressed?
options: A standard 1 to 5 score for every objective
Pounds for every risk, whatever it affects
Days of float on the stage critical path
The same units as the objective affected
A.why: Impact is assessed in terms of the objectives; if objectives are measured in time and cost, impact is measured in time and cost too.

whyNot.0: Scales may be used, but impact relates to the units of the objective affected.
whyNot.1: A time objective is affected in days, not pounds.
whyNot.2: Float is a scheduling concept, not the measure of impact.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Risk [?] is a neutral concept because it can be positive or negative.
options: exposure
appetite
tolerance
velocity
B.why: Risk exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk; it is neutral because it can be positive or negative.

whyNot.1: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk taking.
whyNot.2: Risk tolerance is a measurable threshold for each objective at risk.
whyNot.3: Velocity is how quickly a risk would affect objectives.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Proximity is how near in time a risk might occur.
2. Velocity is how likely a risk is to occur.
3. Probability can be estimated from the frequency of occurrence.
4. Exposure applies to threats but not opportunities.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
B.why: Proximity is about timing (1), and probability is often estimated from probability or frequency of occurrence (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: velocity is how quickly a risk would affect objectives.
whyNot.1: Both are false: velocity is about speed, and exposure is neutral.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: exposure can be positive or negative.

B.q: A flood risk might occur in month 10. If it did, the site would close the same day. Which measure describes 'the site would close the same day'?
options: Proximity
Probability
Velocity
Exposure
B.why: How quickly the risk would affect objectives once it occurs is its velocity.

whyNot.0: Proximity is 'month 10': when the risk might occur.
whyNot.1: Probability is how likely the flood is.
whyNot.3: Exposure is the degree an objective is at risk, not the speed of impact.

C.q: During assessment, the project manager looks at all risks together. What is this view called, and what is it compared with?
options: The risk register summary; compared with the stage plan dates
The combined risk profile; compared with tolerance and appetite
The risk management approach; compared with the change budget
The highlight report; compared with work package tolerances
C.why: The assess step includes assessing the combined risk profile: aggregated exposure compared with risk tolerance and the business's risk appetite.

whyNot.0: The register records risks; the aggregated view is compared with tolerance, not stage dates.
whyNot.2: The approach holds procedures, and the change budget funds changes, not risk.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports give the board stage status; the combined profile is compared with risk tolerance and appetite.

C.q: A risk is close (proximity next month) but its effect would build slowly over a year. What does this tell the project manager?
options: Low velocity: impact would emerge slowly after it occurs
Low proximity: the risk is too far away to need a response
High velocity: the risk is due to happen soon
High exposure: the risk must be escalated to the board
C.why: A slow build-up of effect after occurrence means low velocity, even though proximity is near.

whyNot.1: Proximity is near (next month), not distant.
whyNot.2: Timing of occurrence is proximity; velocity is the speed of impact.
whyNot.3: Nothing says exposure breaches tolerance, so escalation is not indicated.

C.q: Which measure tells the project manager how urgent it is to plan a response, and which tells them how much an objective is at risk?
options: Velocity; probability
Probability; proximity
Proximity; exposure
Impact; velocity
C.why: Proximity (how near in time) drives when responses are needed; exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk.

whyNot.0: Probability is the chance of occurrence, not how much an objective is at risk overall.
whyNot.1: Proximity, not probability, is about timing.
whyNot.3: Velocity is the speed of impact after occurrence, not the degree an objective is at risk.

reteach.title: A storm forecast
reteach.question: A storm might arrive on Saturday, and if it does, roads would flood within an hour. Which bit is proximity and which is velocity?

blocks.body: Saturday is the proximity: how near in time the risk might occur. 'Flooded within an hour' is the velocity: once it happens, how quickly it would hurt. The forecaster's percentage is the probability, and the cost of flooded roads is the impact. How much your weekend plans are at risk overall is the exposure.

blocks.text: Proximity answers 'when?'. Velocity answers 'how fast, once it happens?'.

The estimated chance a risk will occur
The time until the risk might occur
The money set aside for responses
test.why: Probability is the estimated chance that a risk will occur.

explain.body: The estimated effect on objectives if the risk occurs, in the objective's own units.

options: How quickly the risk would strike
The chance that the risk will occur
The estimated effect on objectives
The threshold that triggers escalation
test.why: Impact is the estimated effect on objectives should a risk occur.

explain.body: Proximity: when it might occur. Velocity: how quickly it would affect objectives once it does.

test.q: Which measure is new in PRINCE2 7?
options: Risk velocity
Risk proximity
Risk impact
Risk probability
test.why: Risk velocity is a new concept in PRINCE2 7.

whyNot.1: Proximity was already part of earlier editions.
whyNot.2: Impact was already part of earlier editions.
whyNot.3: Probability was already part of earlier editions.

explain.body: The degree to which an objective is at risk. Neutral: can be positive or negative. Aggregated exposure is compared with tolerance.

test.q: Why is risk exposure called a neutral concept?
options: It is set by the business layer
It is not recorded in the register
It excludes the probability of a risk
It can be positive or negative
test.why: Exposure is neutral because it can be positive (opportunity) or negative (threat).

whyNot.0: The business sets risk appetite, not exposure.
whyNot.1: Individual exposure is not a register heading, but that is not why it is neutral.
whyNot.2: Exposure reflects probability and impact; neutrality refers to its direction.
